title: Into College, Out of Poverty? Policies to Increase the Postsecondary Attainment of the Poor
research_question: Does reducing the financial cost of attending college increase postsecondary enrollment, persistence, and degree completion among low-income students? Which specific design features of cost-reduction programs—such as program simplicity, targeting, eligibility rules, and pairing aid with academic support services or performance incentives—most effectively raise educational attainment for the poor?
data_description: The chapter synthesizes evidence from a wide range of U.S. and Canadian studies covering roughly the early 1970s through the late 2000s. Data sources reviewed include the October Current Population Survey (1969–2000), the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979, High School and Beyond, the Survey of Income and Program Participation (1986–1996), the Survey of Occupational Change in a Generation (1973), U.S. Census files, the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), state administrative records (e.g., California, DC, Massachusetts, West Virginia), Department of Education FAFSA records, SAT records, and program-specific administrative datasets. Units of observation are typically individual students or recent high school graduates. Key variables include college enrollment, choice of institution (2- vs. 4-year, public vs. private, in- vs. out-of-state), credits attempted/earned, GPA, retention, degree completion, loan debt, and hours worked, along with measures of grant/loan eligibility and dollar amounts.
institutional_context: U.S. postsecondary subsidies are large and varied: federal Pell Grants (~$13.6B in 2004–05) and Stafford Loans (~$55B) dominate, supplemented by state subsidies to public universities, state merit scholarships (e.g., Georgia HOPE, Arkansas, West Virginia PROMISE, California Cal Grant, Massachusetts Adams, DC Tuition Assistance Grant), federal tax credits and savings vehicles, veterans' benefits (GI Bills), the now-defunct Social Security student benefit, and private programs (Gates Millennium Scholars, Kalamazoo Promise). Programs differ sharply in targeting and complexity: need-based federal aid requires the lengthy FAFSA, while state merit programs often require only a high school GPA threshold. Recent interventions at community colleges and non-selective universities (Opening Doors, STAR, Upward Bound, H&R Block FAFSA assistance) bundle aid with mentoring, learning communities, counseling, or performance incentives, motivating comparisons across program designs aimed at low-income students with high dropout risk.
